list.name: FaultLine
list.subtitle: Regression and leak-evidence CLI
list.purpose: Replays a frozen, human-reviewed check across Git history in Docker sandboxes to find the first reliable PASS→FAIL commit.

seo.title: FaultLine — Regression and leak-evidence CLI
seo.description: A Go CLI that replays a frozen, human-reviewed check across Git history in Docker sandboxes to find the first reliable PASS→FAIL commit.

notes: Rewritten in Go from the original TypeScript version.
caseStudy.problem: A bisect result or a CI log says where a check failed once. It does not give another engineer evidence they can verify without rerunning the repository's code.
caseStudy.decision: Freeze one human-reviewed check, replay that exact check across the selected Git states in Docker sandboxes, and package the recorded results so another engineer can verify them offline.
caseStudy.constraint: Proof artifacts must never carry credentials, so verification fails closed.
caseStudy.example: Input: a frozen workflow check and four Git states from FaultLine's own history. Output: PASS at e8e30649, the first stable FAIL at 97c3290e, and PASS again at the fix, 07ee7f11, in a package that verified against its recorded root.
caseStudy.rejected: Git bisect on its own: it finds a boundary but leaves no reviewable, portable record of what was executed.
built: A solo Go CLI that replays a frozen, human-reviewed check across Git history in Docker sandboxes. It pinpoints the first reliable PASS→FAIL commit in 1–5 minutes.

It automates investigation, minimisation and CI attestation with GitHub Actions and Sigstore. This saves 1–3 hours per regression investigation compared with manual bisecting, on small-to-medium projects.
Adversarial secret scanning with 8 detection rules plus an entropy heuristic, and fail-closed verification. Together they block credential leaks from proof artifacts.
caseStudy.limitations: It shows where a frozen check first fails across the supplied Git states. It does not establish a unique root cause or an agent's intent.

media.alt: FaultLine's read-only proof page, headed 'Where this frozen predicate first failed', reporting 18 declared files checked, 9 recorded executions, 3 Git states and 2 stable transitions.
media.caption: The read-only proof view of a verified package. It checks every declared file before rendering and never reruns repository code.

media.alt: A Codex session log: FaultLine confirmed the human freeze, then refused to localise the regression without a digest-pinned runtime image.
media.caption: FaultLine inside a Codex session on a real CI failure. After the human freeze it refused to run without a digest-pinned runtime image, a fail-closed stop rather than a guess.

list.name: Gemini Teleportal
list.subtitle: Voice-controlled desktop AI agent
list.purpose: Streams phone audio and screen video to the Gemini Live API, which drives the Windows desktop by exact UI element ids.

seo.title: Gemini Teleportal — Voice-controlled desktop AI agent
seo.description: A voice-controlled desktop agent built with Kai: phone audio and screen video stream over WebRTC to the Gemini Live API, which drives the Windows UI.

caseStudy.team: Built together with Kai; the repository is under his account. Made for the Gemini Live Agent Challenge.
caseStudy.problem: Driving a Windows desktop from a phone usually means pinching at a small mirror of the screen. The aim was to say the task instead, and have an agent that can see the screen carry it out.
caseStudy.decision: Stream phone audio and the desktop's screen over WebRTC to the Gemini Live API, and have a ReAct agent act on exact UI element ids from the Windows UI Automation tree rather than on pixel guesses.
caseStudy.constraint: Pairing had to need no setup: the phone and the desktop find each other through the same Google account, with no QR codes or session URLs.
built: A ReAct agent that clicks exact UI element ids from the Windows UI Automation tree and from annotated screenshots, with perceptual-hash verification. It completed 90%+ of demo desktop tasks unaided.

Phone audio and screen video are streamed over WebRTC to the Gemini Live API. The agent acts on spoken commands within about 2–5 seconds. Pairing needs no configuration, using Google OAuth and Firestore signalling.
A GitHub Actions and Cloud Build pipeline that auto-deploys every frontend change to Cloud Run.

list.name: CircuitMindAI
list.subtitle: PCB inspection
list.purpose: Images in, voice-guided inspection steps out, with cached results for network loss.

seo.title: CircuitMindAI — PCB inspection
seo.description: Nova Pro analyses the PCB image; Nova Sonic talks the operator through the fault. Next.js and Express on ECS Fargate.

caseStudy.problem: An operator inspecting a board needs to see the copper fault and hear inspection guidance, including when the network drops. A detector that fails with connectivity loss is not dependable enough for the inspection floor.
caseStudy.decision: Vision on the board and voice for the operator; results are cached locally so the floor can keep working when the network drops.
caseStudy.constraint: The inspection has to survive a dropped network.
caseStudy.example: Input: a board image and operator audio. Output: a fault overlay on the copper, with inspection guidance still audible when the network drops.
caseStudy.rejected: A server-only detector, rejected because it would fail when connectivity drops.
built: A multi-modal GenAI pipeline: Nova Pro handles vision-based fault detection, and Nova Sonic provides low-latency, two-way voice guidance for the technician.
A decoupled Next.js frontend with an Express REST API.
GitHub Actions builds and pushes Docker images to ECR and updates ECS Fargate on every push. An Application Load Balancer and Auto Scaling keep it available and cost-efficient.
A local cache that holds the inspection when the network drops.
caseStudy.limitations: Detection quality (precision, latency, confusion) was never measured.

media.alt: CircuitMindAI inspecting a PCB photo: components U2 and U3 are outlined, and the model's diagnosis flags thermal discolouration on IC U1 as a warning.
media.caption: Nova Pro's diagnosis beside the board, with the fix-it, voice and agent panels on the right.

list.name: RexCheck
list.subtitle: DeFi pool health scoring
list.purpose: New DeFi pools in, a health score and a trade recommendation out, for a live dashboard and for AI agents.

seo.title: RexCheck — DeFi pool health scoring
seo.description: A Python worker ingests new GeckoTerminal pools; Rails scores them with XGBoost or rules and serves a live dashboard and MCP tools for agents.

caseStudy.team: Built with Chang Kai Zhe; both of us committed to the repository.
caseStudy.problem: A new liquidity pool can be drained within hours of launch. Someone about to trade it, or an agent about to recommend it, needs a risk read in the first hour, not after the fact.
caseStudy.decision: Split ingestion from judgement. An async Python worker polls GeckoTerminal, drops pools it has already seen with a Bloom filter, and queues the rest in Redis. Rails 8 scores each pool, keeps its history in PostgreSQL, pushes it to the dashboard over Turbo Streams, and answers agents through an MCP server.
caseStudy.constraint: Only what a pool shows in its first hour can feed the score.
caseStudy.example: Input: a pool address and network. Output: a 0–100 health score, SAFE, WARNING or DANGER, a recommendation such as DO_NOT_TRADE, and flags such as critical_low_liquidity or wash_trading_suspected.
caseStudy.rejected: A single-page frontend: the dashboard is server-rendered Hotwire, so a new scan reaches the page without a client app.
built: An asyncio ingestion worker with a scalable Bloom filter for duplicates and back-off on GeckoTerminal rate limits.
A risk calculator that scores with an XGBoost classifier on five first-hour features, and falls back to liquidity, wash-trading and pool-age rules when the model is unavailable.
A live Hotwire dashboard, with the N+1 query on the pool list removed by tracking each pool's latest scan.
An MCP server with tools to analyse a token, get a pool's status, list tracked tokens and check the backend, with a static fallback when Rails is unreachable.
Dockerfiles for running the Rails app and the worker as separate ECS Fargate tasks.
caseStudy.limitations: The classifier's near-perfect test scores come from the training pipeline's labelled set, which it can generate synthetically; they are not a measurement on live pools, so none is quoted here. The 500-user MCP load test is written but has no recorded run.
caseStudy.changeNow: Label real pools that were drained, measure the classifier against them, and run the load test.

list.name: Veridian
list.subtitle: MLOps tradeoff engine
list.purpose: Intercepts Terraform and Kubernetes and recommends a lower-carbon compute configuration before provisioning or a demand-driven scale event.

seo.title: Veridian — MLOps tradeoff engine
seo.description: GitLab Duo intercepts Terraform; Vertex AI recommends a lower-carbon compute configuration; BigQuery keeps the carbon ledger off the request.

caseStudy.problem: Selecting compute after provisioning or a demand-driven scale event means remediation arrives after the expensive decision has already been made.
caseStudy.decision: Inspect Terraform before provisioning. Vertex AI recommends a lower-carbon compute configuration. The carbon ledger stays off the request path.
caseStudy.constraint: The ledger had to stay off the request path so a slow or missing carbon number could not stall a provision.
caseStudy.example: Input: a Terraform intent. Output: a recommended compute configuration, with the carbon ledger written beside the request, not on it.
caseStudy.rejected: Putting the ledger on the request path, which would stall provisioning; and selecting compute after provisioning, which arrives too late.
built: GitLab Duo plus MCP intercept Terraform and Kubernetes changes.
Vertex AI recommends a quantised, lower-carbon compute configuration.
BigQuery holds the ESG ledger, off the request path.
caseStudy.limitations: The evaluation period, sample size and emissions-calculation source were not recorded.

teaser.headline: The learned evaluator underperformed PeSTO by 143.3 ±35.4 Elo at 50,000 nodes/move across 128 games.
teaser.annotation: I published the loss, the confidence interval, and what failed.

article.title: The learned evaluator underperformed PeSTO by 143.3 ±35.4 Elo at 50,000 nodes/move across 128 games
article.description: Gate C: a 768×2×256 net lost −143.3 ±35.4 Elo to handcrafted PeSTO at 50,000 nodes/move over 128 games; SPRT terminated for H0.
article.dek: N = 128 games. SPRT terminated for H0.
article.hypothesis: Two evaluations, one search: would the playing 768×2×256 net — trained on 20 million quiet CC0 Lichess cloud evals, depth-12 labels — beat handcrafted PeSTO at the same node budget?
article.disclosure: What was tested as “Learned” is not the net alone: it is the material count plus the net’s output, clamped to ±60 centipawns. The net can adjust a position by at most 0.6 of a pawn either way.
article.experiment: Same search implementation. Fixed 50 000 nodes a move. The first 100 games on the fifty-opening suite stopped short of a bound (LLR −2.33 vs ±2.94). A continuation wrapped the suite until SPRT hit a bound. H0 = 0 Elo, H1 = +10 Elo.
article.failed: LEARNED scored 2 wins, 74 draws, 52 losses in 128 games. LLR −2.99 against bounds ±2.94 terminated for H0. Gate A at the same cap was 0.0 Elo (17–66–17, every pair 1–1), so the −143 is not a colour or adjudication artefact. The retrained net lost harder at 50k than the v1 128 did at 1k. Causal ablations that isolate model capacity, training recipe, or features were not run.
article.causes: Two explanations fit equally well and neither was isolated: the quality of the training data, and the integration itself, where a ±60 centipawn clamp on top of material leaves the net little room to change a decision.
article.learned: A loss at the spec cap is still a result. Do not compare Gate C at 50 000 nodes with the earlier −100 at 1 000 nodes — that was the v1 128. Do not rematch this net: a new net still has to pass the data and progress gates first.
credits: Handcrafted evaluation: the PeSTO piece-square tables by Ronald Friederich.
Lichess eval database, CC0-1.0. No Stockfish network weights are copied.

game.commentary: I built models that had to be interpreted, deployed, and retrained every morning — not fitted once for a screenshot. The knight invites the centre forward: the ML line rather than the systems line.

game.label: 1…e5
game.title: Meeting e4 with e5
game.fact: The classical answer: product engineering on one wing, the data path on the other.
game.commentary: The classical answer. I did not decline into a closed system. Product engineering on one wing, the data path on the other.

game.label: 2. Nf3
game.title: First Developed Piece
game.fact: Petronas, Project Engineer Intern (Internship), Nov 2024 – Feb 2025. Replaced MATLAB-dependent back-end calculation and reporting functions with Python packages, removing paid runtime dependencies.
game.commentary: Knights before bishops, they say. Petronas was the first industry square — I replaced MATLAB-dependent back-end calculation and reporting functions with Python packages, then wrote post-release acceptance cases for the migrated features.

game.label: 2…d5
game.title: The Elephant Gambit
game.fact: Distributed Lead Scorer, Large-scale data mining pipeline. Solo, May 2025. Scores conversion on a hundred million events a day, with checkpoints so a failed hour can resume.
game.commentary: A hundred million events a day had to keep moving even when a job died mid-run. 2…d5 is that impatience, with the checkpoint so the sacrifice is not a bluff.

game.label: 2…d6
game.title: The Philidor, Declined
game.fact: After Petronas the MATLAB world was still there — MathCAD, department code, a quieter engineering path with licences already paid.
game.commentary: 2…d6 keeps the position closed. I developed the knight instead. The dashed line is honest: I could have stayed in the MATLAB world, licences already paid. The other life stays on the page as a ghost — visible, declined, and not a regret. I did not stay.

game.label: 2…Nc6
game.title: Defending the Pawn
game.fact: Setel, Software Engineer Intern (Internship), Jul 2025 – Dec 2025. Authorization and capture of stored payment methods on the payment engine, documented so a new developer could follow the path without a walkthrough.
game.commentary: Payment-engine defects could travel all the way to checkout at the pump. I sat on that square and made sure the pawn could not be taken for free.

game.label: 3. Bc4
game.title: Pointing at f7
game.fact: Western Digital, Full-stack Engineer (Contract), Feb 2025 – Dec 2025. Built the lab-operations dashboard used by 50+ lab staff, with WebSocket station-status and model-inference updates under 100 ms of UI-visible latency.
game.commentary: The Italian bishop looks at the weakest point in the castled position. At WD the weakness was watching lab systems by hand. I put a bishop there.

game.label: 3…Bc5
game.title: Quiet Italian
game.fact: CircuitMindAI, PCB inspection. Solo, Mar 2026. Images in, voice-guided inspection steps out, with cached results for network loss.
game.commentary: CircuitMind sees faults in the copper and talks back over a live voice channel. Black develops the same way — vision on the board, voice on the file.

game.label: 4. c3
game.title: Reliability before the break
game.fact: Reliability before the break: 92.5% unit-test coverage on Setel's checkout and capture; a live-status dashboard for 50+ Western Digital lab staff; 99.9% observed uptime in Veridian's Cloud Run evaluation.
game.commentary: c3 is the quiet move that makes d4 possible. I ship the same way: tests and access control first, so the break has something behind it.

game.label: 4…Nf6
game.title: The Knight Comes In
game.fact: MirrorFi, Solana vault strategy platform. Hackathon team of 6, May 2025. A no-code builder for sharing and executing Solana yield strategies across Drift, Jupiter and Meteora. Grand Prize, Solana Megahack 2025.
game.commentary: Grand prize is a symbol. The work was a product: shareable vault lines, a schema people could copy. Then the last minor piece develops.

puzzle.prompt: White to move — find the break.
puzzle.miss: A developing move. The break was d4. — Ed.

game.label: 5. d4
game.title: The Central Break
game.fact: Veridian, MLOps tradeoff engine. Solo, Apr 2026. Intercepts Terraform and Kubernetes and recommends a lower-carbon compute configuration before provisioning or a demand-driven scale event.
game.commentary: You prepare with c3, then you break the centre. d4 is the move this scoresheet hangs on: agents that intercept infrastructure, measurements instead of demos. The double-exclaim is Informant’s, not mine — but I played it.

game.label: 5…d6
game.title: The Closed Centre
game.fact: Multi-Agent GraphRAG, Policy-corpus retrieval. Solo, Oct 2025. LangGraph over an independent university handbook and policy archive, with a vector fallback.
game.commentary: Prerequisites and credit-transfer live as edges, not another vector-only retrieval. Black can refuse the capture and keep the centre closed — the graph is that kind of patience.

game.label: 5…Bb6
game.title: Tucking the Bishop
game.fact: SLM Distillation Engine, Knowledge distillation and fine-tuning. Lab experiment, Jul 2025. A 70B teacher distilled into a 3B student with QLoRA, DeepSpeed and FlashAttention.
game.commentary: Distillation keeps GraphRAG retrieval on a smaller piece, cheaper to keep on the board. The Italian bishop steps back to b6 and still looks at the same diagonal.

game.label: 5…exd4
game.title: Taking on d4
game.fact: The results on this site, each with its owner, evidence type and date:
game.commentary: I would rather show the graph than the slogan. Accepting the pawn is accepting that the numbers have owners.

game.label: 6. e5
game.title: Gaining Space
game.fact: Monash University, Full-Stack AI Engineer (Contract), Nov 2025 – Feb 2026. Built a FastAPI and Neo4j graph service for university regulations with a self-correcting Text-to-Cypher loop.
game.commentary: 6. e5 gains space and asks the knight a question. The Monash contract asked university regulations one: could a graph answer a prerequisite instead of guessing from the nearest paragraph?

game.label: 6…d5
game.title: The Counter-Strike
game.fact: Black strikes back in the centre instead of retreating the knight.
game.commentary: Every good position invites a counter. The answer is to keep developing.

game.label: 7. Bb5
game.title: The Pin
game.fact: Skribble Lab, Software Engineer (Full-time), Jan 2026 – Jun 2026. Owned the Xendit payment-gateway integration end to end, from requirements review through production support.
game.commentary: The bishop pins before it trades. At Skribble Lab I held one path, payments, end to end until it stopped breaking.

game.label: 7…Ne4
game.title: The Outpost
game.fact: Gemini Teleportal, Voice-controlled desktop AI agent. Built with Kai, Mar 2026. Streams phone audio and screen video to the Gemini Live API, which drives the Windows desktop by exact UI element ids.
game.commentary: The knight jumps into the centre with support behind it. Teleportal was built with Kai, and the square only held because both of us covered it.

game.label: 8. cxd4
game.title: Taking Back the Centre
game.fact: Graduated Apr 2026: Bachelor of Engineering (Honours), Software Engineering, Monash University. First Class Honours, Best Graduate Award, Dean's List.
game.commentary: White takes the pawn back and the centre with it. Graduating closed the file that 1. e4 opened.

game.label: 8…Bb4+
game.title: Check
game.fact: The bishop gives check.
game.commentary: The position asks for an answer before anything else.

game.label: 9. Bd2
game.title: The Calm Block
game.fact: White blocks the check with a developing move.
game.commentary: The calm answer is usually the right one.

game.label: 9…Bxd2+
game.title: The Trade
game.fact: Black trades bishops, with check.
game.commentary: Trading keeps the tension honest. White recaptures next.

game.label: 10. Nbxd2
game.title: The Deepest Move
game.fact: Deriv, AI Engineer (Full-time), Jun 2026 – present. Shipped a full-stack customer-support system that proactively resolves user issues.
game.commentary: The recapture develops the last minor piece. Deriv is the deepest White move on the board so far, and the current one.

game.label: 10…Bg4
game.title: The Pin That Waits
game.fact: FaultLine, Regression and leak-evidence CLI. Solo, Jul 2026. Replays a frozen, human-reviewed check across Git history in Docker sandboxes to find the first reliable PASS→FAIL commit.
game.commentary: The bishop pins the knight and waits. FaultLine does the same with a regression: it holds one question still until the history answers it.

game.title: The Open File
game.fact: The scoresheet stands. What the next move writes is still to be played.
game.commentary: Rooks belong on the open file. The work already points there; the next move is still to be written.

game.label: 4. O-O
game.title: Castling
game.fact: The earlier mainline castled here. It is kept as a variation so older links still land.
game.commentary: Castling is not a retreat. It is the move that says king safety before the central break. I ship the same way — tests and access control before the spectacular sacrifice.

game.label: 4…Nf6
game.title: The Knight Comes In
game.fact: Part of the earlier castled line.
game.commentary: The same knight, one move later in the story.

game.label: 5. d4
game.title: The Break, Castled
game.fact: Part of the earlier castled line.
game.commentary: The same break, with the king already tucked away.

game.label: 5…exd4
game.title: Taking on d4
game.fact: Part of the earlier castled line.
game.commentary: Black accepts, as in the mainline.

game.label: 6. Re1
game.title: The Open File
game.fact: The earlier mainline ended here. The outlook now sits after 10…Bg4.
game.commentary: The rook still belongs on the open file; the game simply went further.

open.body: The learned evaluator lost to PeSTO.
open.qualifier: Controlled benchmark, 128 games at 50,000 nodes a move
open.lede: I trained a chess evaluator, then made it play the handcrafted one.

notes.head: HANDCRAFTED
notes.text: PeSTO piece-square tables, by Ronald Friederich. Each column is what a knight is worth on that square.

notes.head: LEARNED
notes.text: A small net I trained: 768 inputs, two 256-wide halves, 32, then one number.
The same alpha-beta search on both sides. Only the judgement at the end of each line changes.

notesPhone.head: HANDCRAFTED
notesPhone.text: PeSTO piece-square tables, by Ronald Friederich: what a knight is worth on each square.

notesPhone.head: LEARNED
notesPhone.text: A small net I trained: 768 inputs, two 256-wide halves, 32, then one number. The same search runs on both sides.

notes.head: THE DATA
notes.text: Positions labelled with public Stockfish evaluations, from the Lichess evaluation database (CC0). No Stockfish weights are copied.

notes.head: WHAT FELL AWAY
notes.text: Anything a leaf evaluation should not be asked to judge: 15.4 million positions, 43%.

notes.head: TO SCALE
notes.text: 35,405,130 read. 20,040,000 kept. 40,000 of those held out for testing.

notesPhone.head: THE DATA
notesPhone.text: Positions labelled with public Stockfish evaluations from the Lichess database (CC0). No Stockfish weights are copied. 15.4 million fell away through the eight filters below.

notes.head: THE SCORE UNDER EACH
notes.text: How closely the net's judgement matches Stockfish on 40,000 positions it never saw. 1.0 would be perfect.

notes.head: HOW
notes.text: PyTorch. Quantisation-aware from the second epoch, exported to int8, run in WebAssembly inside a worker. 410 KB.

notes.head: NOT A COPY
notes.text: A net that copies PeSTO can never beat it. This one agrees with PeSTO at 0.70, well short of 1.0.

notesPhone.head: THE SCORE BESIDE EACH
notesPhone.text: Agreement with Stockfish on 40,000 unseen positions; 1.0 is perfect. With PeSTO it is only 0.70: not a copy.

notes.head: FIRST, CHECK THE REFEREE
notes.text: Handcrafted against itself: 100 games at 50,000 nodes a move. The same 50 openings, each played once from each side.

notes.head: DEAD LEVEL
notes.text: 17 wins · 66 draws · 17 losses. The harness is fair, so any later gap belongs to the evaluator.

notesPhone.head: FIRST, CHECK THE REFEREE
notesPhone.text: Handcrafted against itself: 100 games, 50,000 nodes a move, the same 50 openings from each side.

notesPhone.head: DEAD LEVEL

notes.head: LEARNED AGAINST HANDCRAFTED
notes.text: Same search, 50,000 nodes a move, the same 50 openings from both sides. Set to stop the moment the evidence was decisive.

notes.head: STOPPED AT GAME 128
notes.text: The evidence crossed the line: LLR −2.99, past the −2.94 bound. The learned net lost.

chapters.voice: A loss at the spec cap is still a result.

notes.head: WHAT FAILED
notes.text: “Learned” was the material count plus the net, and the net was clamped to ±60 centipawns. It could never move a position by more than 0.6 of a pawn.

notes.head: TWO CAUSES, NEITHER ISOLATED
notes.text: The quality of the training data, or this integration. I cannot yet say which.

notes.head: NEXT
notes.text: Do not rematch this net. A new one passes the data and progress gates first.

colophon.purpose: An analysis board: the career as facts, the commentary kept apart, and a chess engine you can actually play.
colophon.publishing: All content lives in typed files in the repository. The same files feed every page, the résumé PDF, the structured data, the sitemap and the preview images. A change goes live with a git push; every pull request gets its own preview deployment for review first. There is no content management system.
tests: Every number on the site is registered in one claims ledger, with an evidence type, an owner and a date.
The hero carries no metric, +45% and +35% are never merged, and −50% appears only under Monash.
Every chess move is legal under the engine's own move generator, the mainline equals the canonical line, and every old ?move= link still resolves.
The résumé PDF fits one page in both paper sizes, is tagged, and renders −, →, ± and é as text.
No engine file or worker loads until the engine is started; a keyboard move gets an engine reply.
With WebGL off every board stays a printed diagram and no 3D code loads; with reduced motion nothing animates.
Every public page has zero automated accessibility violations and no sideways scrolling at 320 px.
colophon.engine: Move generation, alpha-beta search, the handcrafted PeSTO evaluation and a learned NNUE evaluation are written from scratch in TypeScript. The net was trained on CC0 Lichess evaluations, exported with quantisation-aware training and runs through a small WebAssembly module. It starts only when you ask, runs in a Web Worker and pauses when the tab is hidden.
credits: Handcrafted evaluation: the PeSTO piece-square tables by Ronald Friederich.
Lichess eval database, CC0-1.0. No Stockfish network weights are copied.
Chess pieces are glyphs from Noto Sans Symbols 2 (SIL Open Font License).
The 3D pieces are turned from profiles written in code and the mat is drawn in code: no third-party models, scans or textures.
The 3D board uses three.js, React Three Fiber and drei; motion uses GSAP and Lenis; the board state is kept in Zustand.
Built with Next.js, React and Tailwind CSS; hosted on Vercel with cookieless Vercel Web Analytics.
